doc.title: Ray Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Why the family moved to Los Angeles in 1939
summary: Economics and his father's aging career in Chicago drove the move; they hoped for studio work rather than life on the road.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: So, gee moving from Chicago to the west coast, it was like a big thing. Did you want to?

Oh yeah. It was economics. I mean like you’re talking about the Depression and all that, and in those days, well I guess any days, I’m talking about my dad, when you get older, they want new faces and stuff, and he’d been around Chicago for so long. He didn’t want to travel because he was a real family man, like it got to, in the late 30s, the bands just went on the road, that’s the only way, you couldn’t stay in one place. And he didn’t want to do that because he had kids. And the jobs kept getting, the status kind of went down over the years, and he thought well maybe he could start out here. But I think he really had myself, and I have an older brother who sang, he had us in mind, if we’re going to start our career that would sure be a good place to start, in Los Angeles. So that was another one of the reasons.
What was the reputation of Los Angeles at that time?
Well ‘39, oh sure, this was just like the reputation now, I mean as far as being a center for the entertainment, I mean the studios were — out here, I mean I’m talking about Los Angeles.
It wasn’t so much the live music?

Oh no. The studio work, yeah. I guess by that time we all knew that’s the most secure place to be, I guess he thought — he wasn’t hoping for me to be on the road the rest of my life either, which I mean I would have loved to go and play in a swing band. But it’s funny they never — they didn’t say don’t, but I think they had in mind that it would be better if I could get into the studios, that would be much better.
Instead of crisscrossing the country on a train or in a bus.
You know, even, I guess especially like with Goodman and Miller and all those guys. What were they, four weeks maybe in one place? Not for any length of time.
Some of the, like the Basie band or whatever, they’d be more one-nighters even so it had to be tough.

Yeah, well even in my dad’s day it’s like you’d play a location for four to six weeks. And of course back east you would do one-nighters in the summertime. Like during the winter you’d be four or six weeks here, and then jump around. And during the summer months you’d go on one-nighters.
